extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Walt Whitman; writers and critics of 19th-century American literature
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from Walt Whitman's essays and sketches offering aesthetic, social, and practical principles about American literature, storytelling, and national character. Useful as source guidance for producing or evaluating democratic, 19th-century American literary prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-classes: two classes of literature
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain purposes, literary productions may be roughly divided into two classes: (1) a small number (a score or two, perhaps less) of typical, primal, representative works that are different from any before and embody their own main laws; (2) the innumerable writings that are radiations, offshoots, or imitations of the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-class works 'have their own laws, and may indeed be described as making those laws, and amenable only to them.' Whitman (quoting/echoing Margaret Fuller) warns that printing and reading many books does not necessarily mean a nation 'has, therefore, a literature.' Aim for primal originality rather than prolific imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality: make new works that establish their own laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest literary works are those that are 'different from any before' and that 'embody in themselves their own main laws and reasons for being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspire to create works that set their own standards and modes rather than merely following established fashions or producing derivative variations. Such works become the benchmarks to which later radiations relate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate inherited legacies into a modern American physiognomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should receive the accumulated 'precious legacies—accumulations' from Egypt, India, Greece, Rome, medieval and modern Europe cheerfully, and 'give them ensemble, and a modern American and democratic physiognomy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than attempting to imitate Old-World monuments or styles wholesale, adapt and synthesize global literary inheritance so that it acquires a distinctively American, democratic character and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature should build living democratic forms, not merely emulate monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of trying to emulate Europe's cathedrals, ruins, statues, and past monuments, America 'has more than those to build'—vaster and subtler living democratic forms, and the national bards should work for that grand future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that reflect living democratic life and future-oriented, popular forms over works that merely replicate old monumental or aristocratic models. The literary mission is to help shape active national identity rather than to reproduce inherited memorials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value first-hand, earth-based life as a purifying literary source
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'a subtle something in the common earth, crops, cattle, air, trees, &c., and in having to do at first hand with them, that forms the only purifying and perennial element for individuals and for society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground literary depiction in concrete, agrarian, and everyday experience; such first-hand contact with the land and common life supplies durable moral and aesthetic material that resists mere show or artificiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate moral, spiritual, and esthetic elements beyond ostensible wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ostensible wealth, luxury, and show 'imperatively necessitate something beyond—namely, the sane, eternal moral and spiritual-esthetic attributes, elements.' The State cannot flourish without those elements, and they will enter into sociology and literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting modern society and its material successes, writers should also foreground the moral, spiritual, and aesthetic qualities that give life meaning; literature should counterbalance materialism with ethical and soulful depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling and indirection as rhetorical/creative tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote: Lincoln often used story-telling as a weapon and indirection when he could not give a point-blank reply — these indirections were often the best responses possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ narrative anecdotes, indirection, and illustrative stories as effective rhetorical devices in prose and public speech; indirect approaches can reveal truths and defuse tensions more persuasively than direct assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of publication is not equivalent to true literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Margaret Fuller: 'It does not follow that because the United States print and read more books, magazines, and newspapers than all the rest of the world, that they really have, therefore, a literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literary culture by the presence of foundational, original works and lasting artistic achievement rather than by the sheer quantity of printed material. Quality and originality trump productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of common people and democratic voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman values the emergence of leaders and worth from the 'masses'—mechanics, working men, 'heroic, shrewd, fully-inform'd, healthy-bodied' common people—and foresees their centrality in national life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In producing democratic literature, center the perspectives, experiences, and voices of common people rather than exclusively elite viewpoints; authenticity of popular experience strengthens national literature and makes it genuinely democratic.
